name: System Prompt Design
question: What does the model need to know before the first message?
summary: The system prompt is the agent’s standing brief: who it is, what it is for, what it knows, the rules it must follow, when to use each tool, the exact output format, and what to do when it is unsure. Clear sections, explicit reasons for rules and no contradictions matter more than clever wording. Put stable text first so it can be cached, and variable data and the question last.
useCases: Every agent: it is the first thing to get right
Agents with several tools that are easy to confuse
Outputs that feed code, audits or customers

items.detail: who the agent is, who it serves, what success looks like
facts it needs, such as products, policies and dates
what it must and must not do, with the reason
when to use each tool and when not to
the exact structure, or a schema for structured outputs
when to ask, refuse or escalate instead of guessing

steps: Write sections: role, context, rules, tools, format, uncertainty
Explain why each rule exists, and remove contradictions
Put stable text first and variables last, for caching and focus
Test on real cases and fix the failures, one change at a time
pitfalls: Rules added over months that now contradict each other
Vague instructions such as “be helpful” with no definition of done
Putting the user’s data before the instructions in long prompts, or timestamps at the top that break caching
remember: Say who, what, rules with reasons, tools, format, and what to do when unsure.
caption: Illustrative: a support agent’s accuracy with a vague prompt against a sectioned one.

code.text: You are the billing support assistant for a mobile operator. You help
prepaid and postpaid customers understand charges and fix billing problems.
- Never reveal another customer's data: verify the number belongs to the caller.
- Do not promise refunds above Rs 500, because only the billing team can approve them.
- get_bill: postpaid bills and itemised charges.
- get_recharges: prepaid recharge history. Never use get_bill for prepaid.
At most 4 short sentences, then one line: "Next step: ...".
If the plan type is unclear, ask. If a tool fails twice, hand over to a human.

steps.title: State the role and the goal
steps.text: Who the agent is, whom it serves and what a good outcome is. Without this, every later rule floats free of purpose.

steps.title: Write rules with reasons
steps.text: “Because only the billing team can approve them” lets the model handle refund cases the rule did not list. Rules without reasons get applied too literally or not at all.

steps.title: Say when to use each tool
steps.text: The two billing tools were being confused. One line each on what the tool is for, and one explicit “never”, fixes most tool-choice errors.

steps.title: Pin down the format
steps.text: A maximum length and a fixed final line make replies consistent and easy to check automatically.

steps.title: Say what to do when unsure
steps.text: Asking when the plan type is unclear, and handing over after two tool failures, replaces confident guesses with safe behaviour.

steps.title: Stable first, variables last
steps.text: The system prompt never changes between calls, so it can be cached. The customer’s details and question go in the message, last, where the model reads them just before answering.

pros: Cheapest and fastest lever on quality
Cacheable when stable text comes first
Improves tool choice with a few lines
cons: Long prompts cost tokens on every call without caching
Rules accumulate and start to conflict
Wording changes can have surprising effects
Not a security boundary on its own
avoidWhen: Using the system prompt as the only defence against injection or misuse
Stuffing per-request data into the system prompt, which breaks caching

practice.scenario: A telecom operator’s support agent kept confusing its two billing tools and guessed when it did not know a customer’s plan. Its prompt was one paragraph that had grown by accretion. The team rewrote it in sections: role and goal, product facts, rules with reasons, when to use each tool, the exact reply format, and what to do when unsure. Accuracy on the eval set rose from 66% to 90%.

industries.use: A support agent that must choose between billing, plan and outage tools correctly
A service assistant with firm rules about what it may and may not disclose
A tutor that must hint rather than give answers, and escalate distressed students

practice.analogy: A handover note for a new colleague: who you are here, what the job is, what never to do and why, which system to use for what, and whom to call when stuck.

library.name: Anthropic Python SDK
library.what: System prompts go in the system parameter; structure them with clear sections or XML tags, and keep variable data out of the stable part.

practice.note: Every rule states a reason or a limit the model can act on. Put per-request data in the messages, not in the system prompt.

samples.code:
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

SYSTEM = """<role>
You are the billing support assistant for a mobile operator. You help prepaid
and postpaid customers understand charges and fix billing problems.
</role>
<rules>
- Never reveal another customer's data; verify the number belongs to the caller.
- Do not promise refunds above Rs 500: only the billing team can approve them.
</rules>
<tools>
- get_bill: postpaid bills and itemised charges.
- get_recharges: prepaid recharge history. Never use get_bill for prepaid.
</tools>
<format>
Reply in at most 4 short sentences, then one line: "Next step: ...".
</format>
<when_unsure>
If the plan type is unclear, ask. If a tool fails twice, hand over to a human.
</when_unsure>"""

def reply(customer_context: str, question: str):
    return client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929", max_tokens=400,
        system=SYSTEM,                                  # stable: cacheable
        messages=[{"role": "user",
                   "content": f"<customer>{customer_context}</customer>\n{question}"}])

numericDrill.question: A system prompt has 1,230 tokens of stable text and 60 tokens of per-request data. The data is moved from the top to the end, so the stable prefix can be cached. With cache reads at 0.1× the input price, what share of the prompt’s input cost remains per call, in percent? (Ignore the one-off cache write.)
numericDrill.answer: Cached: 1,230 × 0.1 = 123 token-equivalents; uncached: 60. Total 183 of 1,290, or about 14.2% of the original input cost. Putting the variable data at the top would break the cache on every call.

interview.question: What belongs in a system prompt, and what does not?
interview.answer: It holds the standing brief: role and goal, stable context, rules with reasons, tool guidance, output format and what to do when unsure. Per-request data such as the customer’s details and the question belong in the messages, after the stable text, so the prompt stays cacheable and the model sees the question last.

interview.question: Why explain the reason for a rule?
interview.answer: A reason lets the model apply the rule to cases the wording did not anticipate and weigh it against other rules. “Never promise refunds above ₹500 because only the billing team can approve them” generalises better than “no refunds above ₹500”.

mistakes.mistake: Adding rules for every incident until they contradict
mistakes.fix: Review the prompt as a whole and remove conflicts

mistakes.mistake: Putting a timestamp or user name at the top
mistakes.fix: Keep variable data at the end so the prefix can be cached

quiz.question: A billing assistant keeps using the postpaid bill tool for prepaid customers. What is the most direct fix in the system prompt?
options: Add tool guidance saying when to use each tool, and never get_bill for prepaid
quiz.explanation: Explicit tool guidance fixes most tool-choice errors.

quiz.question: Which rule will generalise better to cases it does not list?
options: “No refunds above ₹500, because only the operations team can approve them.”
quiz.explanation: A reason lets the model apply the rule sensibly to new cases.

quiz.question: A system prompt starts with “Current time: 14:32:07”. What is the main cost?
options: The model gets confused about time
The prompt prefix changes every call, so it is never cached
quiz.explanation: Variable text at the start defeats prefix caching.

quiz.question: A prompt has 1,230 stable tokens and 60 variable tokens at the end. Cache reads cost 0.1× the input price. What share of the input cost remains per call? (Ignore the cache write.)
Which belong in a tutoring agent’s system prompt? Select all that apply.
options: What to do when a student seems distressed
The rule to hint rather than give answers, with its reason
Today’s date and time to the second
quiz.explanation: Standing rules and escalation belong in the system prompt; per-request data goes in messages.

quiz.question: Two rules in a prompt contradict each other on rounding. What happens?
options: The model always follows the first
The model picks unpredictably, so outputs become inconsistent
quiz.explanation: Contradictions produce inconsistent behaviour; resolve them.

quiz.question: Which section most reduces confident wrong answers when information is missing?
options: An uncertainty policy: ask, refuse or hand over when unsure
quiz.explanation: Telling the model what to do when unsure replaces guessing.

quiz.question: For a long contract plus a question, what order usually works best?
options: The contract first, then the question at the end
Split the contract across several messages at random
Put the question inside the contract
quiz.explanation: Long documents first and the query last tends to improve use of the context.

quiz.question: Which make a system prompt easier to maintain? Select all that apply.
options: Clear sections such as role, rules, tools, format
Adding a new rule after every incident without review
Copying the same rules into five different prompts
quiz.explanation: Structure and reasons help; unreviewed accretion and copies drift into contradiction.

quiz.question: A prompt says “be helpful and concise”. What is the main weakness?
options: It does not define what a good answer or done looks like
quiz.explanation: Vague goals leave the model guessing; specify the outcome and format.

quiz.question: Is the system prompt a security boundary?
options: Yes, instructions there cannot be overridden
No: it guides behaviour, but controls must also exist outside the model
quiz.explanation: Prompts help but must be backed by real controls.

quiz.question: A prompt rewrite raised accuracy from 66% to 90%. How should the team confirm it? Select all that apply.
options: Measure both versions on the same fixed test set
Check format compliance and escalation, not only accuracy
Ask the model which prompt it prefers
quiz.explanation: Compare on the same data and several metrics.

quiz.question: Where should a customer’s account details go?
options: At the top of the system prompt
In the user message, after the stable instructions
quiz.explanation: Per-request data goes in messages, keeping the system prompt stable.

quiz.question: A prompt of 1,930 tokens, 90% cached, costs $94 a month. Removing 700 tokens of examples leaves accuracy above target. What is the likely effect?
options: Cost falls, with accuracy still on target
quiz.explanation: Examples that do not earn their tokens are paid on every call.

quiz.question: Which are good ways to state rules? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Specific rules with reasons are followed more reliably.

quiz.question: Why use XML-style tags such as <rules> and <format> in a prompt?
options: They are required by every API
They make sections clear to the model and to maintainers
quiz.explanation: Tags separate parts of the prompt clearly.

quiz.question: A prompt gives format rules only in prose, and 30% of replies miss the required final line. What helps most?
options: A dedicated output-format section with the exact structure
quiz.explanation: An explicit format section raises compliance.

quiz.question: Which statements about system-prompt length are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Every token is paid on each call unless cached
Longer prompts are always more accurate
Caching makes length irrelevant for quality
quiz.explanation: Length costs money and does not guarantee quality.

quiz.question: An agent calls a tool that fails twice. What should the prompt tell it to do?
options: Hand over to a human or explain the problem
quiz.explanation: A clear fallback beats loops or invention.

quiz.question: Which change is most likely to break prompt caching?
options: Adding a line at the end of the user message
Changing a word in the first paragraph of the system prompt
quiz.explanation: Any change early in the prefix invalidates the cache.
